what: Tutor Perini is a large US construction contractor. It builds civil infrastructure such as bridges, tunnels, highways and transit systems, and large buildings such as hospitals, airports and casinos, and has specialty contracting units for electrical and mechanical work.
customers: State and city transport agencies, transit authorities, airports and private developers of large buildings, mostly in California, New York and the West.
money: Bridges, tunnels, highways and transit, mostly for public agencies.
Large buildings such as hospitals, airports, casinos and offices.
moat: A small club of contractors can bid on multi-billion-dollar tunnels and bridges, which need bonding capacity, specialised equipment and decades of experience. Tutor Perini is one of them, which limits competition on its largest jobs.
risks: Fixed-price contracts mean cost overruns land on the contractor; the company lost money in 2022, 2023 and 2024.
Large disputes with public agencies over who pays for overruns have tied up cash for years.
Gross margin is thin: $648M on $5.5B of revenue in 2025, which leaves little room for mistakes.
Results depend on a handful of very large projects.
opportunities: Cash of $1.1B is more than double its $477M of debt, after years of collecting old disputed payments.
Revenue reached $6.25B over the last twelve months, the highest in the period shown.
Operating cash flow of $839M over the last twelve months is large against a $4.6B market value.
Infrastructure spending and the backlog of large transit projects give years of work.
watch: Gross margin on new projects, which shows whether the company is winning work at better prices than in the past.
view: Tutor Perini spent three years losing money on old contracts and fighting public agencies for payment, and the shares were priced like a company that might never earn a decent return. That has changed. The losses stopped in 2025, revenue is up sharply, and the cash it fought for has arrived: $1.1 billion on the balance sheet against $477 million of debt, and $839 million of operating cash flow over the last twelve months.

The trailing P/E of 33 is misleading in both directions. Earnings are still depressed by charges on old work, which is why the forward P/E is only 15, and the cash flow overstates normal earnings because some of it is collected disputes. The honest measure is the margin on new contracts, which the company says it now prices with more protection against overruns.

This turns on execution. If the new projects deliver the margins management promises, today’s price is reasonable and the analysts’ $118 target is plausible. If another large job goes wrong, history suggests it will cost hundreds of millions. I think the balance sheet now absorbs a mistake, which it could not before, but I would keep the position small: construction contractors rarely reward investors for long.
bull: New contracts priced with better terms lift margins, and the cash pile funds buybacks.
bear: A large project overruns again and the earnings recovery stalls.
